title: Visual Experience Platform
short: An online classroom for looking at art together
role: Product, UX/UI design, and front-end development
linkText: See the VXP at the Barnes
stack: React, GraphQL, AWS Chime, IIIF deep zoom
body: When the Barnes moved adult classes online in 2020, nothing off the shelf could carry the Barnes method. Zoom lets you show a painting. It doesn't let a student explore brushstrokes at their own pace while an instructor guides the group's attention across a composition.

So we wrote down what the method requires and built to it: shared attention, instructor-led pacing, deep zoom that doesn't degrade, bounded exploration, accessibility from the start, and reliability. Those constraints produced Focus and Explore: when an instructor focuses the group, everyone sees the same view of a work, and when they release control, students zoom around on their own at full resolution. We moved away from slides early and designed around the rhythm of a Barnes class instead.

As of 2026, since 2023 more than 7,000 students and event attendees have learned on the VXP, across 36,800 hours of online teaching and more than 110 classes. One in five users has been a scholarship recipient or an Art for All Community Pass holder. Research keeps shaping what we build. In 2023, course evaluations showed 42% of students watching flat recordings of live classes, so nineteen research sessions and an A/B test produced Replay, a recording that keeps the canvas explorable, and five learner types we still design for. Replay opened up on-demand courses. Students tell us it works: 80% report high or extremely high impact on critical thinking about art, and 91% say it inspired them to keep learning. This year we also built an AI pipeline that takes an educator's PowerPoint, finds higher-resolution images of the artworks, and turns it into a IIIF presentation they can teach from.

In 2025 the Penn Museum became the first institution to license the platform, and a graduate program with Saint Joseph's University runs on it too. A year of supporting another institution showed us where to scale, so fifteen interviews and an effort-by-impact matrix produced the roadmap for VXP 2.0, which shipped in September 2026 with a redesigned admin experience. One platform now supports live courses, on-demand courses, and licensing, and together they fund our mission and access. I built the pricing, onboarding, and support model behind that licensing.

title: Barnes Focus
body: The Barnes hangs no wall labels. Dr. Barnes arranged the collection in ensembles so you'd look at relationships of color, light, line, and space instead of reading a placard and moving on.

Focus is how a visitor can go deeper without putting text back on the wall. You point your phone at a work, it recognizes the work, and the interpretation lives on the device. In June 2026 we replaced the commercial engine behind it with our own, built in weeks rather than the year we would have scoped. The average scan now matches in 594 milliseconds, roughly five times faster, and 61% of first-time visitors have used Focus. That kind of project used to be out of reach for a small museum team, before AI tools came into our workflow.

title: Calder Gardens
short: A whole digital ecosystem for a brand-new institution
body: As operating partner to Calder Gardens, the Barnes team took designs from Karlsson Wilker and brought them to life. The brand guidelines covered the main site. Ticketing, membership, giving, and retail all still needed a design language, so extrapolating from a striking, abstract identity to flows people could move through without thinking about them was my favorite part of the job.

Underneath, it's two front doors and one back office: one codebase and one ticketing pipeline serve both institutions. We planned for multiple brands before the partnership was formalized, which is why a second institution didn't mean doubling the engineering. The site also has a multilingual, AI-powered search that answers visitors' questions from our own content.

title: Membership
short: A portal, digital cards, and renewals people finish
role: Product, UX/UI design, and front-end development
body: The member portal started as a contactless option after reopening: buy tickets, show your card, get updates. I redesigned it that fall and it became the groundwork for everything after.

Redesigning the join and renewal flows, with renewal upsells inside the portal, grew renewals and member engagement. Membership is a digital product with a lifecycle, and it works better when we treat it like one.

title: Commerce
short: Tickets, memberships, and gifts on one stack
role: Product, UX/UI design, and front-end development
body: Almost everything a museum sells or asks for runs through the same few screens: a ticket, a membership, a donation, a class. My team builds and maintains those online flows on ACME for the Barnes and Calder Gardens.

When Calder Gardens opened it needed all of that under its own brand, so one codebase deploys twice, with one ACME tenant and one customer data layer underneath. Two front doors, one back office. That's also what made Plus admission possible: one ticket to both institutions, composed at purchase and put back together at the gate.
We keep our ACME client open source, so any museum on the platform can use it.

title: Deep Zoom
short: Close looking, down to the brushstroke
body: We built a custom IIIF deep-zoom pipeline that tiles artworks through an AWS Lambda and S3. It runs on the online collection and the VXP, where it keeps pan and zoom in sync during live classes so an instructor and a room full of students can look at the same few inches of paint.
Every painting on this site is served the same way. The covers are assembled from the Barnes's public IIIF tiles in your browser, so you're looking at that pipeline right now.

title: Online Collection
short: Search the Barnes Collection by color, light, line, and space
body: The Barnes collection site lets you sort by color, light, line, and space, the four plastic means of the Barnes method. I've built on it since 2021, including the brand work, the 404 and tour pages, and the shared style guide that grew out of it.
This fall the team moved the whole site to Lambda and CloudFront with no downtime, and rebuilt measurement on GA4 so we can see what people do there.

title: Tours and Eye Spy
short: Room by room tours and scavenger hunts on the collection site
body: The collection site also carries tours and Eye Spy scavenger hunts, in English and Spanish, ordered by the rooms you walk through.
Each one is a single config file, so adding a new tour doesn't touch the front end.

title: One Visitor, One Record
short: Moving the Barnes from Raiser's Edge to Salesforce
body: In 2024 I managed our CRM move from Raiser's Edge to Salesforce, and most of my time went to getting Advancement, Marketing, and Guest Services aligned on our data and on the customer journey they share. Now we're working toward a single integration layer. ACME handles tickets, membership, events, and classes, Salesforce holds donor and member relationships, and Brevo runs email, with a data lake connecting them so a visitor is one record instead of three. That's what lets us recognize a member at checkout and see who's calling as the call connects, and it lets staff ask and answer questions through MCP connectors and AI-assisted reporting.
